item.title: The inner fetter and the outer fetter — Beings are entangled in these fetters. I ask Gotama about this: Who can escape these fetters? (The…
item.description:
The inner fetter and the outer fetter —
Beings are entangled in these fetters.
I ask Gotama about this:
Who can escape these fetters?

(The Blessed One):
One established in virtue, wise,
Developing mind and wisdom,
Ardent and discreet —
That monk can escape the fetters.
One who has abandoned greed,
Hatred, and ignorance,
The defilement-free arahant —
He has escaped the fetters.
Where name-and-form is destroyed
Without remainder,
Where the hindrance and perceptions of form are destroyed —
There the fetters are cut.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23

item.title: Elder Parāpariya: Most bodies, Full of pus and blood, Are made by skilled people Into beautifully painted boxes. Bitter as sweetness, Suffering bound by the…
item.description:
Elder Parāpariya:

Most bodies,
Full of pus and blood,
Are made by skilled people
Into beautifully painted boxes.

Bitter as sweetness,
Suffering bound by the agreeable —
Like a sharp sword smeared with honey —
The greedy person does not know.

One who lusts after female form,
Female taste, female touch,
One who is infatuated by female smell,
Meets many sufferings.

All the streams from women —
Five kinds flow in five places —
A person with energy and strength
Can block them.

One who has a goal, abiding in Dhamma,
Skilled, clear-seeing,
Rejoices in doing the duty
Connected with Dhamma and meaning.

Sunk in temporary benefits,
Abandon what is unbeneficial.
If one thinks of such a thing,
Not the thing to be done —
That one, not heedless,
Sees clearly.

If it is a good deed to do,
Rejoice in practicing the Dhamma.
Seize the doing immediately —
That is truly the highest happiness.

With high and low means,
Deceiving others,
Killing, causing sorrow,
Violent, overpowering others —

As a strong man carves wood,
Driving out a peg with a peg,
So the good person,
Drives out a sense-faculty with a sense-faculty.

Developing faith, energy, concentration,
Training mindfulness and wisdom,
Using five to conquer five,
Stainless, one goes forward.

That brahmin, having a goal,
Abiding in Dhamma,
Following the Buddha’s instruction,
Complete, with full strength —
That person enjoys peace.

From: Theragāthā 16.2

item.title: “Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When…
item.description:
“Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is an establishment of consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is a production of future renewed existence. When there is future renewed existence, future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.38

item.title: Elder Siṅgālapitar: “Look at the forest of Bhesakaḷā! A monk lives there, Heir to the Buddha’s teaching, Pervading this great earth With the perception of…
item.description:
Elder Siṅgālapitar:
“Look at the forest of Bhesakaḷā!
A monk lives there,
Heir to the Buddha’s teaching,
Pervading this great earth
With the perception of a skeleton.
I think that monk will quickly
Abandon sensual lust.”

From: Theragāthā 1.18

item.title: "O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes…
item.description:
"O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the eye faculty, practices the restraint of the eye faculty."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta

item.title: “If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘I am not attached to it.’ He understands: ‘I do not delight…
item.description:
“If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘I am not attached to it.’ He understands: ‘I do not delight in it.’ If he feels a painful feeling … If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘I am not attached to it.’ He understands: ‘I do not delight in it.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. When he feels a feeling ending with the body, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling ending with the body.’ When he feels a feeling ending with life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling ending with life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, after death, everything that is felt, in which he no longer delights, will become cool right here.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.7

item.title: “Householders, if those wanderers of other sects ask you: ‘By what basis, by what tradition, do you speak of those venerable ones as follows: Surely…
item.description:
“Householders, if those wanderers of other sects ask you: ‘By what basis, by what tradition, do you speak of those venerable ones as follows: Surely those venerable ones are free from lust, or are on the path to subduing lust; free from ill-will, or on the path to subduing ill-will; free from delusion, or on the path to subduing delusion?’—when asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects: ‘Those venerable ones dwell in remote lodgings in isolated forests. But in such places there are no forms cognizable by the eye that they could see and then delight in; no sounds cognizable by the ear … no odors cognizable by the nose … no tastes cognizable by the tongue … no tangibles cognizable by the body that they could feel and then delight in. Good sirs, by this basis, by this tradition, we speak of those venerable ones as follows: Surely those venerable ones are free from lust, or are on the path to subduing lust; free from ill-will … free from delusion, or on the path to subduing delusion.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 150 – Nagaravindeyyasutta

item.title: “Here, monks, a person truly understands the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures. By truly understanding…
item.description:
“Here, monks, a person truly understands the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures. By truly understanding them, sensual desire, sensual delight, sensual attachment, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, sensual fever, sensual clinging, sensual craving regarding sensual pleasures do not invade and remain. This, monks, is called freedom from the yoke of sensual desire.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.10
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “This city is built of bones, Plastered with flesh and blood; Within dwells aging and death, Conceit and hypocrisy.” “Even the king’s splendid chariot wears…
item.description:
“This city is built of bones,
Plastered with flesh and blood;
Within dwells aging and death,
Conceit and hypocrisy.”

“Even the king’s splendid chariot wears out,
So too this body eventually ages.
But the Dhamma of the good does not age —
So the good indeed speak to the good.”

“A person of little learning,
Like an ox, grows old;
His flesh increases,
But not his wisdom.”

From: Dhammapada 146-156

item.title: “Sunakkhatta, suppose there is a very poisonous viper. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering.…
item.description:
“Sunakkhatta, suppose there is a very poisonous viper. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. What do you think, Sunakkhatta? Would that man give his hand or his foot to that viper if he knew: ‘If I am bitten by this snake, I will meet death or deadly suffering’?”
“No, venerable sir.”
“So too, Sunakkhatta, a monk should surely guard himself in regard to the six sense-bases. Knowing that ‘Attachment is the root of suffering,’ he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment. It does not happen that he would still focus his body on attachment or direct his mind to attachment.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 105 – Sunakkhattasutta
